name: Ascension

lead: In looksmaxxing slang, ascension means a marked rise in perceived attractiveness, and to ascend is to undertake one. Members post plans, protocols and progress updates with before-and-after photos on looksmax.org, and the word is used for gains reached through changes like body-fat loss, skin, hair and style.

The term is a label for an outcome, so there is no single treatment or study behind it. Members describe combining several changes at once, depending on their plan, and some describe strong emotional reactions to looking better.

paras: People set a plan, usually combining changes such as fat loss, skincare, haircut and grooming, fitness, and in some cases dental or surgical work or hormones, then document progress with consistent photos over months.
Risks depend entirely on the methods used, and some methods carry documented medical risks covered in their own entries. Some forum posts note that ascension does not cure psychological issues.

web.title: Fact Check Team: What's looksmaxxing? - KATV

angle.text: Ascension is the community word for a big improvement in looks over time, built from steps such as fat loss, skin, hair and style, with before-and-after photos documenting progress. It names an outcome rather than a method, and the results shown are individual self-reports.

lead: Ascension is looksmaxxing community slang for a substantial improvement in a person's looks, and the verb ascend is used for someone undertaking one. It works as a goal-setting frame: members write ascension plans with target years, post protocols with promised before-and-after photos, and keep long progress updates on looksmax.org [1][2][3][4]. Coverage of the scene describes ascending as each step up the attractiveness hierarchy toward the top tier, and notes that people pursuing harder interventions use the word for any appearance improvement [5].

The term is not a procedure, product or theory. It names an outcome that members pursue through very different routes, from skincare, grooming, fitness and body-fat loss (often called softmaxxing) to dental, hair and surgical work and other medical interventions (hardmaxxing) [6][5][7]. Wikipedia's looksmaxxing article defines ascension as a noticeable increase in status or looks, linking it to softmaxxing techniques [6]. Posts show members using it for emotional reactions as well as appearance, such as one poster describing crying from joy after losing weight and no longer feeling subhuman, a framing other members questioned [1].

No studies examine ascension as such, because it is a label for a result rather than an intervention. Research on the wider looksmaxxing scene is mainly sociological and journalistic, and the surrounding coverage describes the movement's origins on incel-linked forums in the 2010s, its spread to TikTok and YouTube in the early 2020s, and its rise to mainstream attention in 2023 to 2026 [6][7].

paras: Members use ascension both as a noun for the change itself and as a goal-setting frame, as in threads named for an ascension plan with a target year [4]. The scope of what counts varies from a single change such as weight loss to multi-year plans. One Australian news explainer glosses ascending as each step toward the top Chad tier, a term in the community's rating vocabulary, and notes that hardmaxxers use the word for any appearance improvement [5].

A looksmax.org thread titled as an ascension protocol at age 15 shows the term attached to plans made at young ages [8]. Other titles such as a thread on ascension taking time frame the process as gradual [9].

The word belongs to the vocabulary of the wider looksmaxxing scene. Wikipedia reports that looksmaxxing was coined on incel message boards in the 2010s, that three forums, PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net, formed an early community that produced the PSL scale, and that the practice spread to TikTok and mainstream culture in the early 2020s [6]. The same article lists ascension alongside terms such as mogging, softmaxxing and hardmaxxing [6].

A June 2026 Marie Claire Australia feature described a man beating his face with a hammer captioned "Ascend", used to signal an upward progression in a deliberate and dramatic glow-up [10]. The feature also notes the related glow-up genre in which people post transformations, with posts such as one asking others to judge a glow-up and say whether surgery is needed [10]. Mainstream coverage of the internet influencer Braden Peters, known as Clavicular, who rose to prominence on Kick and TikTok in 2025 and 2026, brought the vocabulary of looksmaxxing and ascending to wider audiences [11][5].

Threads include requests for ratings after changes, protocol posts promising before-and-after photos, and reflective posts on the emotions of ascending [1][2][3][12]. The reflective thread cited here treats emotional release as a sign of a significant change, and a reply suggests the poster's weight loss may have influenced his mood [1]. Not all discussion is positive: at least one thread argues that ascension does not resolve psychological problems [12].

A March 2026 Dazed feature described the face-rating channels of a looksmaxxing Discord community, where members have their photos scored on scales such as the 1 to 10 decile and the 1 to 8 PSL, and are steered toward softmaxxing or hardmaxxing recommendations accordingly. It reported that ascending is never presented as finished and that many members feel pressure to keep improving, and a verified rater told the writer people treat him better since improving his looks [13]. Its author also described insecurity and a need for validation as central to the community and linked its rating standards to eugenics-style thinking [13].

Dean Robertson, founder of the Looksmaxxing.com forum, told Marie Claire that attractiveness can change through concrete steps in grooming, skincare, diet and gym work, and that trouble arises when people see their looks as the limit of their worth. He said his forum's surveys found 87 percent of members reported positive life changes and 55 percent reported stress, anxiety or poor mental health [10].

Coverage divides the methods into two broad groups. Softmaxxing refers to skincare, grooming, clothing, gym training and diet, and sometimes less conventional practices such as mewing; hardmaxxing refers to more invasive measures including cosmetic surgery, dental work, leg lengthening, off-label drugs and bonesmashing [6][10][7]. Wikipedia and news explainers report that scientists and clinicians dispute the effectiveness of mewing and bonesmashing, and that physicians warn about fractures and nerve injury from the latter [6][5][10].

Individual methods have their own entries in this wiki. Coverage of Clavicular describes him saying he began looksmaxxing at about age 14 and has used testosterone, steroids and fat dissolvers, and notes that a suspected overdose during a livestream in April 2026 led to hospitalisation; these accounts come from the press and his own statements [5][11].

A news fact-check from April 2026 cites unnamed psychologists and a study in Sociology of Health and Illness describing a hegemonic masculine gaze in looksmaxxing communities and a state researchers call masculine demoralisation. It says experts regard the claim that appearance determines success as misleading and lists warning signs for parents such as obsession with appearance, rapid physical changes and social withdrawal [7]. Charlie Sabgir of the Young Men Research Project criticised the messaging of one prominent influencer's paid academy, arguing that its view of appearance as deterministic taps into young men's confusion and alienation [5].

Marie Claire quotes Sydney cosmetic doctor Dr Amy Chahal on the difficulty of telling real from AI-generated beauty goals and her advice to embrace one's own features; doctors quoted there describe bonesmashing as unscientific and unsafe [10].
No studies found. Ascension is a slang label rather than an intervention, so there is no trial of it as such.

lore.intro: Members use the term for appearance outcomes and the emotional meaning attached to them; coverage adds commentary on its ideals [1][12][5][13].

claims.claim: A successful ascension is accompanied by strong emotion and reflection on one's past self.
Ascension does not fix psychological problems.
Improving your looks changes how others treat you.
Ascension proceeds from soft to hard methods as members keep improving.
Ascension can be planned in advance with a protocol and a target year.
Ascension takes time and can be gradual.

timeline.event: The term looksmaxxing is coined on incel message boards; PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net form an early PSL community [6].
Looksmaxxing spreads to TikTok and broader online culture, often framed as self-improvement [6].
Media coverage of looksmaxxing and bonesmashing increases in outlets such as Business Insider, Vice and The Daily Dot [6].
Academic studies examine surgical design, hegemonic masculinity and health risks of looksmaxxing [6].
Dazed publishes a feature on face-raters in looksmaxxing forums [13].
A suspected overdose during a livestream by Clavicular is widely reported; a news fact-check explains looksmaxxing for parents [6][7][11].
The Nightly publishes an explainer defining ascending, mogging and the PSL scale [5].
Marie Claire Australia features glow-up and ascend imagery and quotes forum founder Dean Robertson [10].
